To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the hippocampus is involved in learning novel stimulus representations that support transfer, and 2) individuals with mild hippocampal volume loss show a selective deficit on tasks that measure this ability.

we have developed a new set of behavioral tasks to evaluate hippocampal function in humans, and have shown that individuals with mild atrophy of the hippocampus are impaired at generalizing from familiar to novel stimulus configurations, and that these impairments are associated with hippocampal dysfunction as measured by fMRI.

hippocampal atrophied elderly individuals show selective deficits on tests of generalization that are not observed in non-hippocampal atrophies, that these deficits may be due to a failure to form hippocampal-dependent representations of the stimulus information, and that these tests may be useful for predicting risk for future cognitive decline.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel behavioral assessment tools that can be used to predict risk for Alzheimer's Disease in non-dementedly elderly individuals.
the development of novel behavioral assessment tools to evaluate the functional consequences of damage to the medial-temporal lobe.
developing a better understanding of the functional role of the hippocampus, and how this role may be compromised in the earliest stages in the development of AD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the research described in this application has the potential to lead to a new paradigm for assessing the risk for AD in non-dementing individuals, as well as a novel paradigm for testing new therapeutic approaches in transgenic mouse and human models of AD.

we have developed a novel battery of cognitive tests that may be sensitive to very mild HA in non-dementing elderly, as well as in individuals with mild cognitive decline, and that these tests are based on computational models that provide a strong mechanistic rationale for their use.

our research has identified behavioral tasks that are sensitive to mild hippocampal dysfunction in non-dementing elderly, and that these tasks may be useful for predicting future risk for AD in these individuals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hippocampal-region is important for learning and generalization, and that these processes may be disrupted in the earliest stages in AD, even before cognitive decline is evident.

our computational and behavioral research is providing a new framework for understanding the role of the hippocampus in learning and memory and for developing new behavioral tools for early detection of AD.
the hippocampus and other structures that show pathology in AD are critical for the ability to generalize from familiar to novel information.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the hippocampus and related medial temporal lobe structures are critical to the ability to learn new information that supports later generalization.

computational models of memory function can be used to identify behavioral markers for hippocampal-region function, and to identify specific cognitive processes that are disrupted in aging and Alzheimer's.
computational modeling can be a powerful tool in developing new behavioral tests that can be used for early diagnosis of AD and for preclinical testing of new therapeutic interventions.
